summary.statement: Nothing is sent to the developers: no analytics, crash reports or usage data, and no account with them. The only server the project controls that Email contacts is its GitHub releases page, for updates.
Your mail stays on your computer, and your passwords are in the system's keychain.
Email talks to your own mail servers and GitHub (for updates); everything else it contacts is a service you turn on.
Pictures and other web content in a message are blocked until you allow them, so senders can't see you opened it until then.
Messages are cleaned of scripts and shown in a frame that allows none.
Updates are signed and checked before they're installed.
Some protections can be fooled by a sender who forges headers, and mail on disk isn't encrypted by Email: see the weaknesses.

developer.claim: Nothing is sent to the developers. The only server under the project's control that Email contacts is the GitHub release it checks for updates.

evidence.note: the Updater step sets the only endpoint: the repository's own latest release

developer.verify: List every outgoing connection (see the connections section) and check each one's destination. None may belong to the developers except the updater endpoint, and nothing may carry usage, diagnostics or identifiers to it.
developer.refuted_if: Any analytics, crash-reporting, telemetry or remote-configuration call, or any request to a developer-run host other than the update check.

connections.claim: Email connects to the mail servers you set up, to read mail (IMAP) and send it (SMTP), over verified TLS. It greets SMTP servers as [127.0.0.1], not by your computer's name, which servers would copy into the Received header every recipient sees.
connections.destination: the user's IMAP and SMTP servers
connections.frequency: while Email runs: kept open for new mail, and for each action
connections.control: add or remove accounts in Settings › Accounts

evidence.note: TLS from the first byte, certificates checked against the system's roots (tls_config)
implicit TLS on 465, STARTTLS otherwise

connections.verify: Read connect_inner and tls_config: the connection is wrapped in TLS before anything is sent, and certificates are verified. Read smtp::transport.
connections.refuted_if: A plaintext IMAP or SMTP path, certificate checks turned off, or a connection to a server the user didn't configure.

connections.claim: When you add an account whose server Email doesn't know, it looks up your email domain's MX records in DNS to find the provider.
connections.verify: Find the callers of discover_server: they must all be part of adding an account.
connections.refuted_if: discover_server or another MX lookup is called from sync, startup or incoming mail.

connections.claim: Google and Microsoft accounts sign in through your web browser; Email then exchanges and renews the sign-in with Google's or Microsoft's token service. During sign-in, Email listens on a local port for the browser's answer.
connections.destination: oauth2.googleapis.com, login.microsoftonline.com, and a port on 127.0.0.1 during sign-in
connections.frequency: when you sign in, and to renew the sign-in about once an hour while in use
connections.control: use an app password instead of signing in

evidence.note: the local listener binds 127.0.0.1 only

connections.verify: Read oauth::https and its callers (token exchange and refresh). Read the listener: it binds 127.0.0.1 and closes after the sign-in.
connections.refuted_if: Tokens sent anywhere but the provider's token host, or a listener bound to a non-loopback address.

connections.claim: If you connect Google Contacts, Email syncs your contacts with Google's People API.
connections.frequency: when the address book opens, after you change a contact, and every 15 minutes

evidence.note: the 15-minute timer, only for connected accounts

connections.verify: Check the sync runs only for accounts with a Google Contacts link (google_links), and find what starts it.
connections.refuted_if: A People API call for an account that isn't connected.

connections.claim: If you turn on tags and snooze for a Microsoft account, Email uses Microsoft Graph for them. Marking a message as spam there also reports it to Microsoft.
connections.frequency: every 3 minutes, and when you tag or snooze

evidence.note: reportMessage

connections.verify: Check graph_task and Graph requests run only for accounts with Graph turned on (accounts.graph).
connections.refuted_if: A Graph request for an account without it turned on.

connections.claim: Writing help contacts Anthropic's API only when you ask. It sends your name and address, the subject and the recipients, the message you're replying to, what you've written, and your instruction, with your own API key. In a message's source view, Ask sends the whole message with its headers.
connections.control: it does nothing until you add an API key in Settings › AI

evidence.note: Ask sends the raw message

connections.verify: Find every caller of ai::run and of the ai_run command: each must start from a user's request in the composer or the source view.
connections.refuted_if: Any path from sync, a timer, startup or incoming mail reaches ai::run.

connections.claim: If you choose a sender-picture level, Email looks up a sender's domain: a DNS query for its BIMI logo, then its website's icon. The BIMI record and the website can name pictures on other servers, which are fetched too. Everything goes over HTTPS to public addresses only, never this computer or the local network. Your DNS resolver sees each domain looked up.
connections.destination: the sender's domain, servers its BIMI record or website names, and your DNS resolver
connections.frequency: once per domain, kept 30 days (a miss, 7)
connections.control: Settings › General › Sender pictures: off, contacts, domains you write to, or all

evidence.note: the level decides; Spam rows ask for none
HTTPS only, public addresses only
recipients count only for mail in a Sent folder

connections.verify: Check the default level is off (lib/senderIcons.ts), that sender_icon returns before any lookup for the Contacts scope and for unknown domains at the Known scope, and that icons::get refuses non-HTTPS and non-public addresses for ICONS.
connections.refuted_if: A lookup with the level off, at Contacts, or for a domain outside the chosen level; a connection to a private address; or (at the 'domains you write to' level) a domain counted as written to because of mail that isn't in a Sent folder.

connections.claim: For a Google contact with a photo of their own, Email fetches it once from Google's photo servers, and keeps it.
connections.destination: Google's photo servers (the address Google gives for the photo)
connections.verify: Read contact_photo and card_photo: the URL comes from the synced Google person, and the photo is kept in card_photos.
connections.refuted_if: A photo fetched for an account without Google Contacts, or from an address a message can set.

connections.claim: Pictures and other web content in a message load only after you allow them, for that message, its sender, or the sender's whole domain (the last only for mail your provider confirmed came from there). Then the web view loads them from their servers.
connections.destination: the servers named in a message's pictures
connections.frequency: each time an allowed message is shown
connections.control: Load images / Always load… over a message; Settings › General lists who's allowed

evidence.note: the frame's content policy allows remote images only when allowed

connections.verify: Read buildSrcdoc's content security policy for both cases, and what decides allowRemote. Check the web view can't load remote content another way (CSS, fonts, iframes, link prefetch).
connections.refuted_if: Any remote request from a message before it's allowed, through any element or CSS.
connections.details: The tests cover the stored allow rules, not the frame's content policy that does the blocking. Once a message's pictures are allowed, its pictures can be on any server, including ones on your local network: a content policy can't limit them to public addresses.

connections.claim: For an allowed message, a picture from a plain http:// address that fails over https (the web view upgrades it) is fetched by Email itself over plain HTTP, from public addresses only.
connections.destination: the server named in the picture's address
connections.frequency: once per failed picture, at most four at a time
connections.control: only for messages whose pictures you allowed
connections.verify: Check rescueHttpImages runs only when the message's pictures are allowed, that mail_image refuses non-public addresses and addresses with control characters, and what an email itself can do with the mailimg scheme.
connections.refuted_if: A fetch for a message whose pictures aren't allowed, to a private address, or one an email can trigger with a crafted address.

connections.claim: Email asks the project's GitHub release for a newer version 20 seconds after starting and every 6 hours, and downloads it when there is one.
connections.frequency: 20 seconds after starting, then every 6 hours

evidence.note: the updater endpoint

connections.verify: Check the timer in updates.ts respects the off switch, and the endpoint in build.yml.
connections.refuted_if: A check with updates turned off, or to another endpoint.

connections.claim: AI apps (MCP) reach Email through a socket on this computer only, never the network, in a folder only you can open. Until you turn AI apps on, they get no mail tools; each permission (reading, drafts, organizing, deleting, sending) is a switch of its own, and deleting and sending ask you every time.
connections.destination: a Unix socket in the data folder
connections.verify: Check the listener is a Unix socket (no TCP) in a 0700 folder, and that tool_list and tool calls give nothing until allowed.
connections.refuted_if: A TCP listener, or a tool call that does anything before it's allowed.

third-parties.claim: Besides your own mail servers and GitHub (updates): Google (sign-in, Contacts and contact photos) and Microsoft (sign-in, Graph, and spam reports with Graph) only for the features you use with their accounts; Anthropic only when you ask for writing help; senders' domains, the servers their BIMI records and websites name, and your DNS resolver, as far as the sender-picture level you choose; and the servers of pictures in messages you allow.

evidence.note: derived from the connections section

third-parties.verify: Compare with the connections section and with the completeness search.
third-parties.refuted_if: A connection whose operator isn't listed here.

storage.claim: Folders, message headers, tags, drafts, the address book and the search index of message text are in mail.db in Email's data folder. Your lists of senders and domains whose pictures always load, and whether rules for a whole domain are on, are here too, and stay when an account is removed.
storage.retention: until the messages are deleted on the server, or the account is removed

evidence.note: the schema; body_fts holds message text for search

storage.verify: Read the schema in store.rs and where the database is opened.
storage.refuted_if: Mail data kept elsewhere, or kept after the account is removed.

storage.claim: The messages themselves, and attachments if you keep them for offline use, are in bodies.db.
storage.retention: as long as the message is kept

storage.claim: The log records what Email did and any problems: account addresses, folder and server names, and timings, and which tools AI apps used. No subjects or message text.

evidence.note: an AI app's action is logged as the tool used, not its summary

storage.verify: Search tracing:: and log:: calls for fields that could hold a subject, body text or a password.
storage.refuted_if: A log line that records a subject, message text, a password or a token.

storage.claim: Attachments you open are copied to the system's cache folder for other apps to open, and cleared each time Email starts.

evidence.note: attachment cache directory, removed at startup

storage.verify: Find where opened attachments are written and the startup cleanup.
storage.refuted_if: Opened attachments kept elsewhere, or not cleared.

storage.claim: Attachments of drafts opened from the server are copied into draft-files/ in the data folder, and removed at startup once no draft or queued message uses them.
storage.retention: until the draft is sent or discarded, then the next start
storage.refuted_if: Copies kept after no draft refers to them.

storage.claim: Your choices in Settings and View options are in the web view's own storage, in the data folder.
storage.location: the web view's storage in the data folder
storage.refuted_if: Message content or credentials kept in localStorage.

storage.claim: The web view keeps its own cache and cookies, so pictures you loaded and cookies their servers set can stay on disk.
storage.location: the web view's folders in the data folder (WebKitCache, cookies, storage)
storage.verify: Look at the data folder after loading a message's pictures.
storage.refuted_if: (A description; refuted if the web view keeps nothing.)

storage.claim: Window sizes and the AI-apps settings are small files in the data folder; saved attachments go to Downloads, and exports where you choose.
storage.location: the data folder (window state, mcp.json); Downloads; your chosen export folder
storage.verify: Search for file writes in app/src-tauri/src.
storage.refuted_if: Another file written with user data.

secrets.claim: Account passwords, sign-in tokens, the writing-help API key and your Google sign-in client are kept in the system's keychain (one item, dev.mail-client), never in files, and sent only to the service each belongs to.
secrets.verify: Find where credentials are read and written: only through the vault. Check where each one is sent.
secrets.refuted_if: A credential written to a file or the database, logged, or sent anywhere but its own service.

untrusted-input.claim: Messages are cleaned before they're shown: scripts, event handlers, javascript: links, links to data: pages, and link targets are removed.
untrusted-input.verify: Read the sanitizer's allowed tags, attributes, URL schemes and the attribute filter.
untrusted-input.refuted_if: Markup that survives cleaning and can run script or open a document of the message's making.

untrusted-input.claim: A message is shown in a sandboxed frame whose content policy allows no scripts; links open in your browser, never in Email.

evidence.note: script-src 'none'; <base target=_blank>
the sandbox attribute
navigation outside the app goes to the browser

untrusted-input.verify: Read the sandbox flags, the content policy, and the window's navigation and new-window handlers. No test covers this; it needs checking in each web view.
untrusted-input.refuted_if: Any way for message content to run script, reach the app's IPC, or navigate the app window.

untrusted-input.claim: Remote content is blocked by default. A rule to always load pictures believes a message's From address as far as the account's server checks it. Gmail and Microsoft add their own Authentication-Results header to every message, and other servers can sign theirs with their own name; where the topmost header is one of these, a rule counts only when it confirms the message came from the sender's domain (DMARC, or DKIM signed by it). Elsewhere the header could be the sender's own, so a rule trusts the From address. Rules for everyone at a domain are off unless the user turns them on, and never cover shared mail services such as gmail.com.
untrusted-input.verify: Read get_message and allow_remote_from_domain: when from_believed requires the header's confirmation, how sender_verified and sender_domain reach allow_remote, and that domain rules need the setting.
untrusted-input.refuted_if: Where the account's server checks senders (Gmail, Microsoft, or a topmost header carrying its server's name), a rule applying to mail the header doesn't confirm; a domain rule applying, or one being added, while the setting is off; or a domain rule for a shared mail service.
untrusted-input.details: A server that writes no Authentication-Results lets the sender write one under any name, so a header naming the account's server proves the server checked only if that server removes forged copies of its own (RFC 8601 says it should). Matching a name only ever makes the check stricter, never looser. Existing domain rules turned the setting on when it was added, so they kept working.

untrusted-input.claim: Only known kinds of documents, pictures, sound, video and zip files open directly; anything else (programs, scripts, shortcuts, disk images, web pages, Office files with macros, unknown types) is only saved. File names are cleaned. On Windows and macOS, attachments Email saves or opens are marked as downloaded from the internet (the Mark of the Web, the quarantine flag), so the system warns or opens them in a protected mode.
untrusted-input.verify: Read is_openable (a list of types that open) and where opening checks it.
untrusted-input.refuted_if: A type that can run code opens directly.

updates.claim: Each update is signed with the project's update key and checked against the public key built into Email before it's installed. On Linux, an .rpm update is installed as root (after your password) from a new folder only you can open. The macOS app is signed and notarized by Apple.

evidence.note: Update::download verifies the signature (Tauri's updater plugin)
signing with TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY; the public key built in

updates.verify: Read the updater plugin's download and install path, and updater::install_rpm (which installs with --nosignature after that check).
updates.refuted_if: A path that installs a download whose signature wasn't checked.

supply-chain.claim: Releases are built from the public repository by GitHub Actions. Every action is pinned to a commit and Rust to a version, so the jobs that hold the signing keys run only what was reviewed; Rust and npm dependencies are pinned by their lock files.
supply-chain.verify: Read the workflow: every uses: names a commit, and the toolchain a version; lock files are used.
supply-chain.refuted_if: A uses: by tag or branch, or dependencies fetched unpinned.

permissions.claim: Email uses the network, the system keychain, notifications (on by default, showing the sender and subject; Settings › Notifications), files you choose (open, save, export), and being the default mail app (if you ask; the Linux package registers it for mailto: links at install). It asks for your password to install .rpm updates as root (pkexec). Release builds include the web view's Developer Tools. It doesn't use the camera, microphone, location, the system's contacts, or running at login.

evidence.note: plugins: dialog, opener, deep-link, single-instance, updater; notify-rust

permissions.verify: Read the capability files and the plugins used.
permissions.refuted_if: A permission or plugin not listed here.

weaknesses.claim: Email doesn't encrypt mail on disk: anyone who can read your files can read your mail. Use your system's disk encryption.

evidence.note: plain SQLite

weaknesses.verify: Check the databases are opened without encryption.
weaknesses.refuted_if: (It's a limitation; refuted only if the databases are in fact encrypted.)

weaknesses.claim: Loading a message's pictures tells their senders you opened it, when, and from which address; a plain-http picture's address can also be seen on the network.

Message frames carry allow-scripts and allow-same-origin so the app's own key and link listeners work; only the content policy (script-src 'none') and the sanitizer keep a message's own code from running.
weaknesses.verify: Read the frame's sandbox attribute and the content policy.

weaknesses.claim: Dependencies aren't yet audited automatically for known vulnerabilities (no cargo audit or npm audit in the build), and the Linux and Windows installers aren't signed by the operating system's vendors.
weaknesses.refuted_if: An audit step in the build.

weaknesses.claim: Where the account's server doesn't check senders in a way Email can rely on, 'always load pictures from this sender' trusts the From address as written, which a sender can forge; so does a rule for everyone at a domain, when the user has turned those on.
Once a message's pictures are allowed, they can be on servers on your local network, which the web view will request.
On Linux, saved attachments carry no mark that they came from the internet: Linux has no standard one.
AI apps: one switch turns them on for every AI app, and an app names itself. While off, an app can see that Email is there and a tool saying why no others are available.
This report is written by hand: nothing yet checks automatically that it lists every connection.
weaknesses.verify: Look for a build check comparing the code's connections with this report.
